bullets: How a flower makes a seed: pollen is delivered, the gametes fuse, and the seed travels away
slides.heading: Reproduction: pollination to seed
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we follow one pollen grain on its whole journey - delivery, fusion, and the seed travelling away to grow somewhere new.

bullets: Describe pollination as pollen transfer from anther to stigma, and name wind, water and animals as carriers
Explain fertilisation as the fusion of the male gamete with the ovule, and correct the claim that the two events are the same
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep them apart in your minds, because our exit ticket will ask you to separate delivery from fusion.

bullets: Pollination and fertilisation are always told in the same breath, so they sound like one event
But a pollen grain sitting on a stigma has not fused with anything yet - so what is still missing?
slides.heading: Two events or one?
slides.notes: Ask the class: if pollen has already landed on the stigma, has the flower been fertilised? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because scene 2 shows the step that is still missing.

bullets: Pollination is transfer: pollen moves from an anther to a stigma
Fertilisation is fusion: the male gamete joins the ovule inside the ovary
Delivery must come first, but delivery alone makes no seed
slides.heading: Delivery is not fusion
slides.notes: Stress the two verbs: transfer versus fuse. Pollination moves the package; fertilisation is the joining that happens afterwards, inside the flower.

bullets: Pollen grains travel from flower A's anther to flower B's stigma
Wind, water and pollinating animals all carry the grains
slides.heading: Pollination: pollen on the move
slides.notes: Play scene 1 and pause as the carrier crosses: the grains landing on the stigma complete pollination - and nothing has fused yet.

bullets: The landed pollen grows a tube down the style
The male nucleus travels through the tube and fuses with the ovule - this fusion is fertilisation
slides.heading: Fertilisation: tube to ovule
slides.notes: Play scene 2 and trace the tube growing: fertilisation happens only at the moment of fusion, deep inside the ovary.

bullets: After fertilisation the ovule becomes a seed that must travel away from the parent
Wind lifts seeds, water carries them, animals drop them, and some pods explode
slides.heading: Seed dispersal: four ways to travel
slides.notes: Play scene 3 and name each carrier as it appears: dispersal spreads seeds so the young plants do not compete with the parent.

bullets: The two events are separate: pollination delivers the pollen, fertilisation is the fusion that follows
A flower can be pollinated without being fertilised if no fusion follows
slides.heading: Myth: pollination IS fertilisation
slides.notes: Play scene 4 and ask the class to state the difference in one sentence each: delivery first, fusion second.

bullets: A grain lands on a stigma: pollination is complete, but the tube has not grown and no fusion has happened
So the flower is pollinated, not yet fertilised - the claim fails on this one grain
slides.heading: Worked example: testing the claim on a landed grain
slides.notes: Work it slowly: Step 1, landing is transfer, so pollination is done. Step 2, fusion needs the tube and the meeting with the ovule, so fertilisation has not happened yet.

bullets: In pairs: write one sentence for what pollination does and one for what fertilisation does
Then swap and check: does either sentence use the other event's verb?
slides.heading: Your turn: separate the two events
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes. Listen for transfer words in the pollination sentence and fusion words in the fertilisation sentence, then take two pairs' answers.

bullets: Your exit ticket asks you to correct a student who merges the two events into one
Name delivery and fusion separately to earn full credit
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Point to the exit ticket and remind the class: the strongest answers keep pollination as delivery and fertilisation as fusion.
